module.objective: Mampu mengulas film atau cerita naratif menggunakan participle clauses dan kosakata emosional tingkat menengah.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Stories That Keep Us on Edge
subModules.theme: Cinema, Storytelling and the Psychology of Fear
subModules.grammarFocus: Present, past and perfect participle clauses

content.summary: Read a short film review about a frightening mystery. You will practise finding the main ideas and details, learn words for describing stories and feelings, and notice how participle clauses make a review more concise.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Present participle clauses use an -ing form, past participle clauses use a past participle, and perfect participle clauses use having plus a past participle.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Words for suspense, fear, surprise and emotional reactions in films and stories.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skim the review first to understand its main opinion. Then scan it for names, events and reasons. Use nearby words to work out unfamiliar vocabulary.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short review about a mystery film.
Find details about the film's plot, atmosphere and audience reactions.
Recognize present, past and perfect participle clauses in a review.
Use intermediate vocabulary to describe fear and other strong emotions.

contextWarmup.prompt: What can make a frightening film feel more suspenseful?
options: A slow build-up that makes viewers wonder what will happen
A list of all the actors before the film starts
A bright, cheerful scene with no mystery
contextWarmup.explanation: A slow build-up can create suspense because viewers have time to wonder what will happen next.

rules: Use an -ing clause to show an action or feeling connected to the main clause. The subject is usually the same in both parts: Feeling nervous, Maya entered the cinema.
Use a past participle clause when the subject receives an action: Frightened by the noise, the children covered their ears.
Use having plus a past participle when one action is completed before another: Having read the book, Maya compared it with the film.

commonTrap.explanation: The subject of a participle clause should match the subject of the main clause. Otherwise, the sentence can suggest that the wrong person or thing did the action.
commonTrap.wrong: Walking into the cinema, the film's music frightened Leo.
commonTrap.correct: Walking into the cinema, Leo heard frightening music.

grammarFormulas.title: Sentence Patterns with Participle Clauses
grammarFormulas.description: Use these blocks to notice how a participle clause connects with a main clause. Keep the subject clear.

complements.text: Feeling nervous, Maya entered the cinema.
Frightened by the noise, the audience fell silent.
Having seen the trailer, Maya expected a different ending.

items.exampleSentence: The gripping story kept everyone watching until the end.
A spine-chilling sound came from the empty room.
The final plot twist changed how I understood the story.
The suspenseful scene made us wait to learn who was outside.
I felt overwhelmed by the film's sad ending.
The eerie house stood alone at the end of the road.
We watched a thriller about a missing student.
The soundtrack made the quiet scenes feel tense.
The audience stayed silent during the final scene.
The film is an adaptation of a popular novel.

paragraphs: Last Friday, Maya watched The House Beyond the Lake, a new thriller directed by Ana Reed. The story follows Leo, a young photographer who visits a quiet village to learn about an old family story. Walking along the lake one evening, he sees a light in a house that everyone says is empty. The scene is eerie, but it does not show a monster or a sudden attack.

The film builds suspense slowly. A low soundtrack plays whenever Leo finds a new clue, and the audience begins to share his worry. Frightened by strange noises, he still returns to the house each night. The plot is gripping because each answer leads to another question. Maya says the quiet moments are more frightening than the loud scenes.

Having read the novel before seeing the film, Maya expected the ending to be different. The plot twist surprised her, but she thought it made sense because the director had included small clues earlier. She felt overwhelmed for a moment, then wanted to talk about the story with her friends. Maya recommends the film to people who enjoy suspenseful mysteries, though she warns that it may be too tense for young children.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Cinema Reactions and Horror Psychology

content.summary: Learn how to follow fast post-movie discussions where speakers share immediate reactions, evaluate narrative tension, and use participle clauses to condense details.
learningObjectives: Catch the main topic and emotional reactions in a lively cinema review.
Identify participle clauses used in natural spoken English to describe actions.
Notice consonant-to-vowel linking and consonant drops in fast conversation.

keyPhrases.note: Used informally to say an event or film lived up to high expectations.
An adjective describing an intense feeling of fear or terror.
An unexpected turn of events in the narrative of a book or movie.
Used to describe an emotional or physical shudder from fear or excitement.

connectedSpeech.note: The final /ŋ/ in 'having' often softens to an alveolar /n/ in rapid casual speech.
The final /t/ links directly to the vowel in 'in', and the 'h' in 'her' is dropped.
The unvoiced /t/ sound connects smoothly to the diphthong /aʊ/ without a pause.
The /t/ in 'hot' assimilates into a velar /k/ sound before the /k/ in 'coffee'.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Reviewing Cinema and Suspense with Participle Clauses

content.summary: Learn how to use participle clauses to describe dramatic movie scenes and write engaging film reviews without repeating simple conjunctions.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Present Participle Clauses for Simultaneous Actions or Reasons
blueprintItems.formula: Present Participle Phrase (-ing), Subject + Verb + Complement
blueprintItems.example: Feeling anxious about the strange footsteps, David locked the wooden door.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Past Participle Clauses for Passive Context
blueprintItems.formula: Past Participle Phrase (V3), Subject + Verb + Complement
blueprintItems.example: Shocked by the unexpected plot twist, the cinema audience sat in silence.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Perfect Participle Clauses for Completed Earlier Actions
blueprintItems.formula: Having + Past Participle (V3), Subject + Verb + Complement
blueprintItems.example: Having read the original horror novel, Sarah noticed every small change in the film.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always separate an introductory participle clause from the main clause with a comma.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Hearing a loud scream the detective stopped walking.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Hearing a loud scream, the detective stopped walking.
mechanicsRules.why: A comma prevents confusion and clearly marks where the background action ends and the main action begins.

mechanicsRules.rule: Avoid dangling participles by making sure the subject of the main clause actually performs or receives the participle action.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Running through the dark forest, the old castle frightened the lost travelers.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Running through the dark forest, the lost travelers saw the frightening old castle.
mechanicsRules.why: The castle was not running through the forest; the travelers were.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'Not' directly before the participle to form a negative participle clause.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Did not knowing the secret code, she failed to open the exit.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Not knowing the secret code, she failed to open the exit.
mechanicsRules.why: Participle clauses do not take auxiliary verbs like 'did' or 'do' for negation.

sampleSentences.en: Hearing a sudden whisper behind him, the young guard turned around quickly.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: Describe a Tense Movie Moment
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three to four sentences describing a scary scene in a movie. Use at least one present participle clause (such as 'Hearing a strange sound,...' or 'Looking through the window,...') to describe what happened.
guidedLabChallenges.example: Walking down the dark hallway, the detective noticed an open window. He held his flashlight tightly in his hand. Suddenly, the front door closed with a loud bang.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: Mini Movie Review
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three to four sentences reviewing a suspense or horror movie you know. Include either a past participle clause ('Directed by...' or 'Frightened by...') or a perfect participle clause ('Having watched...').
guidedLabChallenges.example: Directed by a talented new filmmaker, this horror film surprised me with its great acting. Having seen the trailer, I expected lots of cheap jump scares, but the story was actually very clever. I recommend it to anyone who enjoys psychological mysteries.
guidedLabChallenges.placeholder: Write your short film review here...

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine these two sentences into one sentence using a present participle clause (-ing):
practicumQuestions.promptText: She felt exhausted after the long film. She went straight to bed.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'Feeling exhausted...' and remember to add a comma.
targetAnswers: Feeling exhausted after the long film, she went straight to bed.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The present participle 'Feeling' explains the reason and replaces 'Because she felt exhausted', followed by a comma before the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the sentences using a past participle clause (V3) to create a concise passive description:
practicumQuestions.promptText: The thriller was directed by Alfred Hitchcock. The thriller became an instant classic.
targetAnswers: Directed by Alfred Hitchcock, the thriller became an instant classic.
Directed by Alfred Hitchcock, the film became an instant classic.
Directed by Alfred Hitchcock, the movie became an instant classic.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The past participle 'Directed' replaces the passive clause 'The thriller was directed by...' and attaches neatly to the main subject.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using a perfect participle clause (Having + past participle):
practicumQuestions.promptText: After he watched the scary documentary, Tom could not sleep at night.
targetAnswers: Having watched the scary documentary, Tom could not sleep at night.
Having watched the scary documentary, Tom couldn't sleep at night.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The perfect participle 'Having watched' shows that the watching was completely finished before Tom experienced trouble sleeping.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Add the missing comma and correct capitalization in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: screaming in terror the character ran into the abandoned house
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize the first word and place a comma after 'terror'.
targetAnswers: Screaming in terror, the character ran into the abandoned house.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Introductory participle clauses must begin with a capital letter and end with a comma before the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct this dangling participle so that the audience is the subject of the main clause:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Walking into the dark theater, the big screen shocked the audience.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'Walking into the dark theater,' and continue with 'the audience felt shocked by the big screen.' or 'the audience was shocked by the big screen.'
targetAnswers: Walking into the dark theater, the audience was shocked by the big screen.
Walking into the dark theater, the audience felt shocked by the big screen.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The big screen did not walk into the theater. The audience did, so 'the audience' must immediately follow the comma.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine these two sentences into one using a present participle clause instead of 'Because':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Because they heard strange footsteps, the detectives drew their weapons.
targetAnswers: Hearing strange footsteps, the detectives drew their weapons.
practicumQuestions.explanation: You can replace reason clauses starting with 'Because' by using a present participle when both clauses share the same subject.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using a negative present participle clause (Not + -ing):
practicumQuestions.promptText: Because she did not understand the ending of the story, Maya read the book again.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start your sentence with 'Not understanding the ending of the story,'.
targetAnswers: Not understanding the ending of the story, Maya read the book again.
practicumQuestions.explanation: To make a participle clause negative, place 'Not' before the verb without any auxiliary verb like 'did'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite these sequential actions using a perfect participle clause:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Leo bought his cinema ticket, and then he found a seat near the back.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'Having bought his cinema ticket,'.
targetAnswers: Having bought his cinema ticket, Leo found a seat near the back.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The perfect participle 'Having bought' highlights that buying the ticket was completed before finding the seat.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fix the punctuation and capitalization in this film critique sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: impressed by the visual effects critics praised the new sci-fi movie
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize the first letter and place a comma after 'effects'.
targetAnswers: Impressed by the visual effects, critics praised the new sci-fi movie.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A past participle phrase at the beginning of a sentence requires a capital letter at the start and a comma before the main subject.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine these two sentences using a past participle clause:
practicumQuestions.promptText: The audience was terrified by the unexpected sound. They jumped out of their seats.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'Terrified by the unexpected sound,'.
targetAnswers: Terrified by the unexpected sound, the audience jumped out of their seats.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Drop 'The audience was' and start with the past participle 'Terrified' to express the cause compactly.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Film Reviews and Fear

content.summary: Practise reviewing films and telling short stories about suspense and fear. Use emotional vocabulary and participle clauses to connect ideas, for example, 'Feeling overwhelmed, I needed a moment to calm down.'
content.audioGuidance: Speak clearly and give important words such as 'gripping' and 'spine-chilling' extra stress. Use a falling tone for opinions and a rising tone when asking a question. Pause briefly before describing a plot twist.

pillars.name: Clear Word Stress
pillars.target: Stress the correct syllable in longer words
pillars.explanation: Listen for the main beat in words such as 'suspenseful' and 'overwhelmed'. Say the stressed syllable clearly without making every syllable equally strong.

pillars.name: Emotional Expression
pillars.target: Match your voice to the feeling
pillars.explanation: Use a slightly tense voice when describing a frightening scene, then relax your tone when explaining your opinion.

pillars.name: Connected Ideas
pillars.explanation: A participle clause can explain a feeling or action. For example, 'Watching the final scene, I felt overwhelmed.' Keep the subject of both parts clear.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The main stress is on the first syllable of 'gripping' and the second syllable of 'suspenseful'.
The main stress is on the first syllable of 'eerie' and the final syllable of 'overwhelmed'.
Give the first part of 'spine-chilling' strong stress. In 'plot twist', stress both words.
Both words have their main stress near the end, on 'pense' and 'whelmed'.

drills.targetText: The gripping story kept me watching until the end.
drills.phonetic: /ðə ˈɡrɪpɪŋ ˈstɔːri kept mi ˈwɒtʃɪŋ ənˈtɪl ði end/
drills.focus: Stress in 'gripping' and natural sentence rhythm
drills.hint: Make 'grip' and 'watching' clear, then let the smaller words move quickly.

drills.targetText: The eerie house made the whole scene feel unsettling.
drills.phonetic: /ði ˈɪəri haʊs meɪd ðə həʊl siːn fiːl ʌnˈsetəlɪŋ/
drills.focus: Clear vowel sounds and emotional description
drills.hint: Say 'eerie' slowly, then keep the rest of the sentence smooth.

drills.targetText: Feeling overwhelmed, I left the cinema in silence.
drills.phonetic: /ˈfiːlɪŋ ˌəʊvəˈwelmd aɪ left ðə ˈsɪnəmə ɪn ˈsaɪləns/

drills.targetText: Did you expect the plot twist at the end?
drills.phonetic: /dɪd ju ɪkˈspekt ðə ˈplɒt twɪst ət ði end/
drills.focus: Rising intonation in a yes-or-no question
drills.hint: Let your voice rise slightly on 'end'.

roleplay.context: You are speaking with a friend after watching a suspenseful film together. Share your reactions and ask what your friend thought about the ending.

turns.speaker: Friend
turns.text: What did you think of the film? I found the story gripping.
turns.translation: Apa pendapatmu tentang filmnya? Menurutku ceritanya sangat menarik.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I agree. The suspenseful scenes kept me guessing until the end.
turns.translation: Aku setuju. Adegan-adegan yang menegangkan membuatku terus menebak sampai akhir.

turns.speaker: Friend
turns.text: The plot twist surprised me. Did you see it coming?
turns.translation: Perubahan alurnya mengejutkanku. Apa kamu sudah menduganya?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Not at all. Feeling overwhelmed by the ending, I needed a minute to think.
turns.translation: Sama sekali tidak. Karena terbawa emosi oleh akhir ceritanya, aku perlu waktu sebentar untuk berpikir.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 25 seconds about a film or story that made you feel strong emotions.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Tell me about a film or story that you found gripping or frightening.
storyPoints: Say what the film or story was about and where you watched or read it
Describe one suspenseful, eerie, or spine-chilling moment
Explain how you felt and whether you would recommend it
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Watching the suspenseful final scene, I felt overwhelmed by the unexpected plot twist.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈwɒtʃɪŋ ðə səˈspensfəl ˈfaɪnəl siːn aɪ felt ˌəʊvəˈwelmd baɪ ði ˌʌnɪkˈspektɪd ˈplɒt twɪst/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Tell events in a clear order and use emotional vocabulary to explain your reaction.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 25 seconds about a frightening or mysterious story.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Tell a short story about a strange place or an unexpected event.
storyPoints: Describe the place and the people who were there
Explain what strange or frightening thing happened
Say how the story ended and how the characters felt
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Walking into the eerie house, we heard a sound that made us stop.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈwɔːkɪŋ ˈɪntuː ði ˈɪəri haʊs wi hɜːd ə saʊnd ðət meɪd ʌs stɒp/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use past tenses for events and a participle clause to introduce an action.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Take part in a call with a friend. Give your opinion and respond naturally.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Your friend calls after watching a thriller with you.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You and a friend have just watched a thriller. Your friend wants to talk about the story and its ending.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are the viewer who enjoyed the film. Describe what made it gripping and ask what your friend thought.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I found it gripping because the suspenseful scenes kept me guessing.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Give a clear opinion, add a reason, and ask your friend a relevant question.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Take part in a call about a horror film. Describe its atmosphere and react to your friend's opinion.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Your friend asks whether the horror film was scary.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are discussing a horror film by phone. Your friend liked the story but found some scenes frightening.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You thought the soundtrack and setting were eerie. Explain how they affected you.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The eerie music made the empty house feel even more frightening.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Describe the atmosphere and explain how it made you feel.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Take part in a call about a surprising film ending.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Your friend asks if you expected the plot twist.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You and a friend are comparing your reactions to a film's final scene.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You did not expect the twist. Explain what you believed before the ending and how you reacted.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I thought the detective was helping, so the plot twist surprised me.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use past-tense sentences to explain what you thought and what changed.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Take part in a call with a friend who is choosing a film to watch.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Your friend asks you to recommend a film and explain how it might make them feel.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A friend wants to watch a film this evening and asks for a recommendation.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Recommend a suspenseful film, describe its mood, and mention who might enjoy it.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I recommend it if you enjoy suspenseful stories with an unexpected ending.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Make a recommendation and support it with a simple reason.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Use 'gripping', 'spine-chilling', 'eerie', and 'overwhelmed' in spoken sentences about a film.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Describe a film using at least three of these words: gripping, spine-chilling, eerie, overwhelmed.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The eerie setting made the story gripping, and I felt overwhelmed by the ending.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Choose each word to match its meaning and use it in a complete sentence.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Make two sentences using participle clauses to describe a film scene and your reaction.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Begin one sentence with 'Watching the final scene...' and another with 'Feeling frightened...'.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Watching the final scene, I noticed the strange shadow. Feeling frightened, I turned on the light.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use an -ing participle clause and make sure its subject is the same as the subject of the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say 'suspenseful', 'overwhelmed', and 'spine-chilling'. Make the stressed syllables clear.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Repeat each word, then use it in a sentence about a film.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The suspenseful film left me overwhelmed by its spine-chilling scenes.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə səˈspensfəl fɪlm left mi ˌəʊvəˈwelmd baɪ ɪts ˈspaɪnˌtʃɪlɪŋ siːnz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Put the strongest stress on 'pense', 'whelmed', and 'spine'. Keep the other syllables shorter.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Ask one question with rising intonation and give one opinion with falling intonation.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Ask whether your friend expected the plot twist, then say how you felt about the ending.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Did you expect the plot twist? I felt overwhelmed by the ending.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /dɪd ju ɪkˈspekt ðə ˈplɒt twɪst aɪ felt ˌəʊvəˈwelmd baɪ ði ˈendɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Let your voice rise slightly at the end of the yes-or-no question. Use a falling tone to finish your opinion.
